Gloss: there, that way, over there (place is known but invisible); away
Entry_Text: ʌ́l 2 (G, J) adv. ‘there, that way, over there (place is known but invisible); away’. Buṛ éle ‘dort’, Sh. aál (do.), Kal. ála ‘up there’. Ex.: mī̃́ ẓhɑ̄̀ ʌ́l thū̀ ‘my brother is over there’. Cf. Morgenstierne’s discussion of Paš. elo ‘this’ (1973a: 9) and of the Pshṭ local adverbs (1926: 35), e.g., rā-tləl ‘to arrive’, rā-kawə́l ‘hergeben’ (cf. Lorenz 1979: 66). Such Pshṭ formations are structurally identical with J ʌ́l diyʌ́ṽ ‘to throw away’ (see below). Note that the stress shifts to a following postposition (this is, in fact, the only example for this kind of accent shift): ʌl-mʌ̀z ‘over there inside’. Cf. also lɑ̄̀ 2 and ṣʌ́l.

ārùh adv. ‘here; quite close to’. The sufﬁx -ùh (also in pātùh 2, pārùh, etc̣) expresses a local relation to a third implicit or explicit point of reference. This can, but must not, be the case with ɑ̄́r, pɑ̄́th 2, pɑ̄́r 1. Thus, sùh ārùh thū̀ means ‘he is at the side of (a group of people close by)’. Another difference with sùh ɑ̄́r thū̀ (cf. example sub ɑ̄́r) is that ārùh indicates a certain distance between ‘he’ and ‘the group’, thus more exactly: ‘he is quite close to (a group of people which is close by)’. It is possible to further increase the distance between the two points with the help of lʌ̀kh 1 ‘little’: sùh ārù-lʌkh thū̀ ‘he is fairly close...’

ḕ (B) interj. ‘hey!’ The interjection is, e.g., used for calling boys or girlṣ The phonetic shape of the initial vowel and of the whole interjection is sociolinguistically determined, depending on whether the caller is male or female. These are the forms used by a male caller: éṛä ‘hey boy(s)!’ éṛï ‘hey girl(s)!’ And these are the forms used by a female caller: ë́näṛä ‘hey boy!’ ë́näṛï ‘hey girl!’ ë́näṛō̃ ‘hey boys!’ ë́näṛiyū̃ ‘hey girls!’ The forms used by male callers are prob. reduced forms of the female ones which derive from ńā̃ṛ ‘boy’. It is interesting to see that the female callers not only use the ‘bright’ ë́ against the male ‘dark’ é., but that also in the vocative form of ‘boy/girl’ a ‘bright’ pronunciation is useḍ

kʌ́rū, -ō n.m. ‘a lion; a tiger’; kʌ́ro, kʌ́rʒ (Š) n.m. ‘a leopard’. The word is also used to frighten children, but then, it is said, kʌ́rū would mean ‘wild sheep’. In fact, this may be the basic meaning because of Paṛ ɣarō̃ ‘sheep’, Sak. kaura- ‘sheep’, Wkh. kar ‘mouton à courtes oreilles’, Buṛ kíro ‘Schaf (Kindersprache)’, Sh.chil. karɑ̄́ ‘a ram’. The word might be of Dravidian origin, e.g., Tam. kori ‘sheep’ (cf. DED 1799 for Dravidian alloforms and semantic varieties similar to those of Northern Pakistan). Semantically closer related with ‘lion’, however, is Munda-Himalayan (?) Raji ki:ri, ki:ḍi ‘tiger, leopard’ (Sharma 1990: 174) with Munda parallels in Pinnow 1959: 142 ( 281) (but cf. also DED 1059). xodey (G) n.m. ‘God’. Same as J xudḕ. Among Gabār speakers there is a way of associating the ﬁgures from one to ten with basic items: ‘one’ is God; ‘two’: yū̃̀ ā̃ sū̀ri ‘moon and sun’; ‘three’: tʌlɑ̄́q ‘divorce’ (the three exclamations); ‘four’: yārān ‘friends’ (the four companions of Muhammad); ‘ﬁve’: nimāz ‘daily prayers’; ‘six’: kʌlimah ‘articles of faith’; ‘seven’: dōzáq ‘hells’; ‘eight’: žʌntàh ‘paradises’; ‘nine’: duniʌy ‘worlds’; ‘ten’: dʌriāb ‘rivers’. And about ‘eleven’ it is said: kē̃z na pūri ghāsui ‘nobody has completed it’.

Head_Source: ṭùṅgʌr or ṭùṅgur, ṭòṅgrah (G, J, Š) but Š plural ṭùṅgurʒ
Entry_Text: ṭùṅgʌr or ṭùṅgur, ṭòṅgrah (G, J, Š) but Š plural ṭùṅgurʒ adj.m.; n.m. – n.f. ṭuṅgʌ̀ri or ṭuṅgrī̀ ‘hunchbacked; a hunchback’, but Š only n.m. and different meaning ‘hip’. Niš. ṭüŋür-nāṭ ‘ein Tanz in gebückter Haltung (kaﬁṛ)’, Kal. ṭuŋ dyek ‘to bend over or down’. Tam. ṭoṅku ‘crookedness’ (DED 2418), next and ṭóṅg-ṭoṅg.

Gloss: ṭukṭúk (← ṭùk 3 -ṭukh, note change and shift of accent) the Mullah demands a ṭṓk (this word has no clear meaning, but perh. originally meant ‘a morsel
Entry_Text: ṭòk-ṭokh n.m. name of a children’s game: several children sit behind each other with outstretched legs, the ﬁrst puts his arms round the trunk of a tree, the second puts his arms round the ﬁrst child, etc̣ Then a child comes near who is dressed like an adult and who wears a stick, and sings: ṭukṭúk mhōlɑ̄̀ ṭṓk lukhɑ̄̀th = ‘ṭukṭúk (← ṭùk 3 -ṭukh, note change and shift of accent) the Mullah demands a ṭṓk (this word has no clear meaning, but perh. originally meant ‘a morsel’, cf. P. ṭukk ‘a bit of bread’)’. Then the child tears away the last child of the row, and the same is repeateḍ Cf. Pshṭ ṭakṭakā̃ṛai and Pshṭ ṭapṭapā̃ṛai ‘name of a game played by children’.

t̄ rsuz̄́ ṽ (2m) itṛ ‘to writhe (in pain); to yearn (for)’. Pres. itṛ sùh tarsuzɑ̄̀th ‘he writhes (in pain)’. Pres. caus. sùh tarsuzā́th or tarsuziā́th ‘he causes (s.o.) to writhe (in pain)’. Fuṭ and preṭ are regulaṛ Aoṛ itṛ sùh tarsuzìli ‘he writhed (in pain)’. Aoṛ tṛ sʌ́ỹ tarsuzā́ or tarsuzḗl ‘he caused (s.o.) to writhe (in pain)’. Conṭ itṛ sùh tarsùzā̃ bḗt ‘he writhes (in pain) continuously’. Conḍ pres. itṛ tarsuizlū́. Parṭ perf. itṛ tarsuzíli-. The adverbial complement for the itṛ form is constructed with the postp. kirā̃̀ ‘for’. Ex. pres. itṛ: sùh mʌyṭkʌ̀ṽ-kirā̃ tarsuzɑ̄̀th ‘he yearns for the girl’. Originally prob. two separate roots which, however, are now felt by the speakers of J to be one verb. The ﬁrst verb with the meaning ‘to yearn’ also in Uṛ tarasnā ‘to long’, ultimately < tŕṣyati (5942). The second verb with the meaning ‘to (cause to) writhe in pain’ also in P. tarās ‘great alarm’ and Pshṭ tars ‘fear, terror’, ultimately from Perṣ tars ‘fear, terror’.

d,y v̄́̃ 1 (4m) v.t. ‘to give’. Pres. tṛ m. sùh dḗth ‘he gives (s.th. to s.o.)’. Pres. tṛ f. sùh dī́th ‘she gives (s.th. to s.o.)’. Pres. caus. sùh dayā́th ‘he causes (s.o.) to give (s.th. to s.o.)’. Pres. pasṣ sùh dēzɑ̄̀th ‘it is given (to s.o.)’. Pres. caus. pasṣ sùh dēvzɑ̄̀th ‘it is caused to be given (to s.o.)’. But actually used in the sense of ‘to be felt’ (see below)’. Fuṭ tṛ sùh daṣʌ̀th ‘he will give (s.th. to s.o.)’. Fuṭ caus. sùh dayā́ṣʌth ‘he will cause (s.o.) to give (s.th. to s.o.)’. Fuṭ pasṣ sùh dēzàṣʌth ‘it will be given (to s.o.)’. Perf. tṛ sʌ́ỹ dḗ-ċhē ‘he has given (s.th. to s.o.)’. Perf. caus. sʌ́ỹ dayā́-ċhē ‘he has caused (s.o.) to give (s.th. to s.o.)’. Perf. pasṣ sùh deū́z thū̀ ‘it has been given (to s.o.)’. Aoṛ tṛ sʌ́ỹ dḗ or dḗl ‘he gave (s.th. to s.o.)’. Conṭ tṛ sùh dìā̃ bḗth ‘he gives (s.th.) continuously (to s.o.)’. Conṭ caus. sùh dayā̃̀ bḗth ‘he causes (s.o.) continuously to give (s.th. to s.o.)’. Conṭ pasṣ sùh deùzā̃ or deuzā̃̀ bḗth ‘it is continuously given (to s.o.)’. Conv. tṛ dàh-. Conv. caus. dayā́-. Conv. pasṣ deúz-. Conḍ pres. tṛ dēlū́. Conḍ pres. caus. dayālū́. Conḍ pres. pasṣ dēzilū́. Parṭ perf. tṛ díthi-. 1 Parṭ perf. tṛ 2 dḕl-. Parṭ perf. caus. dayḗl-. Parṭ perf. pasṣ dēzíli-. Imp. sg. tṛ dèh. Imp. pl. tṛ dī̃̀. Imp. sg. caus. dayā́. Imp. pl. caus. dayʌ̀ỹ. Imp. sg. pasṣ dēzàh. Imp. pl. pasṣ dēzī̃̀. Subj. tṛ 1. sg. dám, 2./3. sg. dèh, 1. pl. díž, 2./3. pl. dī̃̀. Subj. caus. 1. sg. dayā́m, etc̣ Subj. pasṣ 1. sg. dēzám, etc̣ Adh. tṛ sg. dḗē or dḗyē. Adh. tṛ pl. dī̀ỹē. Pres. caus. pasṣ only with a few nounṣ Ex.: mī̃́-kirā̃ bū́c̣h dēvzɑ̄̀th ‘I am hungry’. The form is apparently the passive of a -v- causative extensioṇ Note also the imperative compound verb da-gʌ́l ‘give!’ built like Uṛ de-do, and the perf. 2 compound verb sùh da-gḕl ‘he has given’. The form of the latter is the result of haplology < PIK *da-galḕl (← galʌ́ṽ). < dádāti (6141).

Gloss: a young (pubescent) girl (twelve to fourteen years old); a virgin
Entry_Text: bʌṭkumɑ̄̀r, -ah n.f. ‘a young (pubescent) girl (twelve to fourteen years old); a virgin’. A typical synonym compound basically meaning ‘girl-girl’. Second element (OIA kumārī́- [3303]) is not inherited but borrowed from one of the Dardic languages where OIA medial -m- is preserveḍ First element < *beṭṭa- (9238). Turner’s quote of Toṛ bat-kumā ‘maid’ sub vṛddhá-2 (12073) is, of course, wrong. Cf. below bɑ̄́ṭ-lakʌ̀y ‘children’ and the similar synonym compound Buṛ/Sh. ćumuṭkér ‘junge Frau’, Kho. and Kal. čhumuṭkēr ‘marriageable girl, maiden’, Wkh. čə;itk;ír ‘femme aux cheveux bouclés; vieille femme parée comme une jeune’ (also Gy. čhumut ‘beautiful girl’). Acc̣ to Berger < *choṭṭa- and kumārī́. However, this is a triple synonym compound: ﬁrst syllable cf. Kal. čhu ‘daughter’ (ﬁrst syllable < duhitŕ.- [6481], second syllable < *maṭṭa- [9723], and third syllable < kuḍa-1 [3245]); the different vowels in čhumuṭkēr are the result of (not uncommon) vowel leftshift and metaphony: at an intermediate stage *čhumaṭukuṛi the second -u- (a dimin. sufﬁx) shifted to the left, producing *čhumuṭkaṛi, and metaphony caused the present form of the ﬁnal vowel (cf. the different etymological interpretation of Bashir 2001: 11f.). Further similar compound formations are: Kam. j’ukuř ‘woman’ ( < duhitŕ.- and kuḍa-1), B dh́ï-bïō̃̀ ‘a woman’ (liṭ: ‘daughter-sister’), nā̃kvüṭ ‘a girl’ (liṭ: ‘wife-girl’), J dhižū́ ‘a daughter’ (liṭ: ‘daughter-daughter’), bng. beṭkuṛi ‘young daughter’ (liṭ: ‘daughter-girl’), Ash. istrimalī-kuṛɑ̈̄ ‘girl’ (a triple compound < strī́- plus mahallikā- plus kuḍa-1 [liṭ: ‘woman-mother-girl’]), and Kal. istrížagúa.k ‘young girl’ (a triple compound < strī́- plus jāyɑ̄́- plus kuḍa-1 [liṭ: ‘woman-wife-girl’]). This type of compound is apparently limited to the NW and to Munda: Sanṭ coṇḍ kuṛi ‘a girl from 8 to 10’ (liṭ: ‘girl-girl’).

biẓō̃́ṛ n.f. ‘rainbow’. Same as bizvā̃́ṛ. < *vīdhradhanus- (12052) despite Fussman’s astonishment over Turner’s reconstruction, “le sens proposé par T. pour ce composé (‘arc dans le ciel bleu’) me paraˆit assez curieux; le propre des arcs en ciel est d’apparaˆitre par le temps de pluie” (Atlas 13). The important point is not that the emergence of a rainbow indeed does require meteorologic conditions where parts of the sky have to be clear, but that the modern form of this word has to be understood as a karmadhāraya- compound and not as a tatpuruṣa- as both authors seem to take for granteḍ The modern representative of vīdhrá- can also mean ‘blue’ in Phal. Thus biẓō̃́ṛ originally meant ‘blue/green bow’. With this meaning it parallels exactly Pshṭ šna kāsa ‘rainbow’ which liṭ means ‘blue/green bow’. Moreover, this semantic pattern for ‘rainbow’ is not uncommon in the area, as there is also Pshṭ sra kāsa, liṭ ‘red bow’, and Woṭ. latúr kasōṭ, also meaning liṭ ‘red bow’.

buḍɑ̄̀ ṭʌ̀ṇḍ˚ (n2) n.m. or verbal: buḍɑ̄̀ ṭaṇḍʌ́ṽ an old custom: in winter youths put on masks, roam wildly through the village and collect eatables; they sing in front of every house with sticks in their hands; their leader has a sack, he is understood to be the “old man” (cf. prec̣), before he gets something he has to dance. The children sing the following: hēṛɑ̄́-tā̃-bēṛɑ̄́ uìṛi-uiṛi makʌ̀y dēṛɑ̄́. This rhyme is also sung by children after maize harvesṭ I noted it down at two occasions, and the two versions display interesting phonetic differenceṣ See the second version with a translation attempt sub makʌ̀y. See ṭaṇḍʌ́ṽ and cf. Buṛ ḍuḍémale hol ‘das Wilde Heer’. In the Buṛ word there may have been an assimilation of initial ḍ- < b-. In Sh.chil. the custom is called buḍī́-buḍā.

Gloss: a type of pheasant or partridge
Entry_Text: bulāš 1, -áh (G) n.f. ‘a type of pheasant or partridge’. Sh. buleéj, Buṛ bulá ‘Ramchikor, Bergrebhuhn, Schneehuhn’. Prob. a lw. and a compound < OIA *bhrūra-vāśuka- or *bhrūralla-vāśuka- (see 9690 and 14800). This reconstruction coincides semantically exactly with Ash. sā̃-waċū́ ‘hen monal pheasant’. Note also Turner’s comment sub śyāmā- (12664) “*hen pheasant, hen golden oriole’ (opposed to bright cock bird ṣv. *lohiṣṭha-)’. The reconstruction is further supported by bng. pɔ.laśɔ, W.Pah. pə.laśe and W.pah.jauṇ p.lássh [sic] ‘pheasant’ which derive < OIA *palita–vāśuka-.

mɑlḕṣ, -ah n.m. ‘a guest’. Related words mostly begin either with man-, men- or with mal-, mel-: Kho. and Kal. menú ‘guest’, Sh.pal. manēṣ (with falling tone) ‘guest’, Buṛ manáac̣ ‘Respekt’, Sh. manáac̣i ‘geehrter Gast’, Š malɑ̄̀ṣ ‘guest’. Some Iranian parallels, esp. Pshṭ (mēlmə ‘guest’), are morphologically quite close to these formṣ Nevertheless do they appear to have at least partially different etymological backgrounds and are not considered here (cf. Morgenstierne 1927b: 44). Assuming a composite IA background for the quoted forms, it seems that the ﬁrst type of initial syllable derives < mɑ̄́na-1 ‘honour’ (10040); the second type of initial syllable is connected with P. melī, mellī ‘a guest at a wedding; a friend’ and thus < mela- (10331); the ﬁnal syllable < yātrika- ‘traveller’ (10457). One thus can reconstruct OIA *mela-yātrika- ‘befriended traveller’ and OIA *māna-yātrika- ‘respected traveller’ (with OIA tr > c̣ [and weakened to ṣ] as in c̣ɑ̄̀ ‘three’).

Gloss: ahead, in front; front; to be ahead
Entry_Text: mṹĩṭhʌṽ adv.; postp.; adj.; v.i. ‘ahead, in front; front; to be ahead’ (Uṛ āge honā, āge huā), cf. mũĩṭhrʌ́ṽ. Ex.: sùh mṹĩṭhʌṽ bḗth ‘he walks ahead; sùh tʌ̀s-mũĩṭhʌṽ bḗth (a) ‘he walks ahead of him’, (b) ‘he goes up to him’; sùh bhɑ̄̀-mũĩṭhʌṽ bhḕṭh thū̀ ‘he sits in front of the house’; sùh mṹĩṭhʌṽ bhɑ̄́-mʌz bhḕṭ thū̀ ‘he sits in the front house’; tùh mṹĩṭhʌṽ ‘be you ahead (of me), you are ahead of me, you (have) proceeded’. This last verbal use is to explained thus: as the etymological derivation below shows, this word (also in its function as a verb) is a derivation from a noun (resp. from the adverbial derivation of the noun). As a hab. verb its inﬁnitive and past participle have the same form in IK. Its use, however, is meanwhile reduced to just two functions, and even the place of the accent is “wrong”: in verbal use the accent normally had to be on the ﬁnal syllable. On the other hand, the -r- causative extension of the verb (see below) has a fully unfolded paradigm. The members of this lemma derive < OIA *mukhasthā-. The word mṹĩṭhʌṽ and its alloforms with the same ﬁnal syllable have an additional derivational sufﬁx. Woṭ. muṭh ‘vor’. Cf. J sāmùṭh and its similar etymology. Note that Sh. muc̣hṓ ‘in front’ does not directly correspond with the basic IK lemma but is an exact parallel to mṹĩṭh-nā̃ because the Sh. word can be decomposed into *muṭ plus ẓhō ‘from’.

Head_Source: lʌ́m-c̣ʌm or lʌ́m-čʌm or lʌ́m-žhʌm 1 or lʌ́m-bʌṛaqh
Entry_Text: lʌ́m-c̣ʌm or lʌ́m-čʌm or lʌ́m-žhʌm 1 or lʌ́m-bʌṛaqh ‘very sharp pain’. Same meaning as c̣ʌ́m-c̣ʌm. l-́̃ (3m) v.t. ‘to reap’. The paradigm displays a complicated behavior of the nasalization which is explained in the grammaṛ Pres. tṛ m. sùh luā̃̀th ‘he reaps (crops)’. Pres. tṛ f. sùh loē̃̀th ‘she reaps (crops)’. Pres. caus. sùh luā̃́th or luyā̃́th ‘he causes (s.o.) to reap (crops)’. Pres. pasṣ sùh lō̃zɑ̄̀th ‘it is reaped’. Fuṭ tṛ sùh lū̃́ṣʌth or lū̃vàṣʌth ‘he will reap (crops)’. Fuṭ caus. sùh lũɑ̄́ṣʌth or lũyɑ̄́ṣʌth ‘he will cause (s.o.) to reap (crops)’. Fuṭ pasṣ sùh lō̃ō̃́sṣʌth (three syllables) ‘it will be reaped’. Perf. tṛ sʌ́ỹ lō̃́-ċhē ‘he has reaped (crops)’. Perf. caus. sʌ́ỹ lũyɑ̄́-ċhē ‘he has caused (s.o.) to reap (crops)’. Perf. pasṣ sùh lõū́z or lõuízi or lō̃úz thū̀ ‘it has been reaped’. Aoṛ tṛ sʌ́ỹ lū̃́ or luī̃́li (note accent) ‘he reaped (crops)’. Conṭ tṛ sùh lùā̃ bḗth ‘he reaps (crops) continuously’. Conḍ pres. tṛ lō̃lū́. Conḍ pres. caus. luiā̃lū́. Conḍ pres. pasṣ lō̃zlū́. Parṭ perf. tṛ lũĩ́li-. Parṭ perf. caus. lũĩḗl-. Parṭ perf. pasṣ lō̃zíli-. Imp. tṛ sg. lō̃́. Imp. tṛ pl. lũī̃̀. Imp. caus. sg. lũyɑ̄́. Imp. caus. pl. lũyʌ̀ỹ. Imp. pasṣ sg. lō̃zàh. Imp. pasṣ pl. lō̃zī̃̀. Sub. tṛ 1. sg. lū̃́m, 2./3. sg. lū̃́, 1. pl. lũī̃́ž, 2./3. pl. lũī̃̀.
